chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from al-Hakam ibn Miskin from Ayub ibn A'yan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A woman was performing Tawaf (circumambulation of the Kaaba) and a man was behind her. She extended her arm, and he reached out with his hand and placed it on her arm. Allah made his hand stick to her arm so that he stopped the Tawaf. The Amir was sent for, the people gathered, and he sent for the jurists. They began to say, 'Cut his hand, for he is the one who committed the crime.' Then someone said, 'Is there one of the descendants of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, here?' They said, 'Yes, al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him) arrived last night.' So he sent for him and summoned him. He said, 'Look at what happened to these two.' He faced the Qiblah, raised his hands, and remained for a long time supplicating. Then he came to her and freed his hand from her hand. The Amir said, 'Shall we not punish him for what he did?' He said, 'No.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a man's hand getting stuck to a woman during Tawaf according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the distinction between judicial punishment (*hadd*) and divine sign (*ayah*), where jurists initially prescribed cutting the hand for the man's physical contact during Tawaf. Imam al-Husayn (peace be upon him) intervened not by overturning the legal ruling, but by invoking divine mercy to remove the physical cause of the 'crime,' thereby sparing the man from amputation. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the Imam's authority to interpret the spirit of the law and the role of supplication in mitigating legal consequences.
